## PROPERTIES OF WHOLE NUMBER
Properties of whole numbers make calculations under operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division easier. The different types of properties of whole numbers are as follows.
## Properties of Addition
## (i) Closure Property
When two numbers a and b are added, the result, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> will also be a whole number.
Therefore, whole numbers are closed for addition.
(ii) Commutative Property
If a and b are two whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. In other words, when whole numbers are added, the order does not matter. This property is called Commutative Property. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow></math>. So, whole numbers are commutative for addition.
## (iii) Associative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and c are three whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> i.e., the manner of associating numbers does not change the result. This property is called Associative Property.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math>
So, whole numbers are associative under addition.
(iv) Additive Identity
Additive Identity is a number which when added to any whole number, then the value remains the same. Let a be any whole number, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. So, 0 is the additive identity of whole numbers.
## Properties of Subtraction
(i) Closure Property
If a and b are two whole numbers such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is a whole number. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is not a whole number.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ?
Therefore, whole numbers are not closed under subtraction.
(ii) Commutative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are two whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is not equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math>. So, the subtraction of whole numbers is not commutative.
(iii) Associative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and c are whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is not equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
So, the subtraction of whole numbers is not associative.
(iv) Property of Zero
If a is any whole number other than zero, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
## Properties of Multiplication
(i) Closure Property
If a and b are whole numbers, then their product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> will always be a whole number.
So, whole numbers are closed under multiplication.
(ii) Commutative Property
When two whole numbers, a and b are multiplied in any order, then their product remains the same. This property is called commutative property. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
So, whole numbers are commutative under multiplication.
(iii) Associative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and c are three whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

(iv) Multiplicative Identity

## PROPERTIES OF WHOLE NUMBER
Properties of whole numbers make calculations under operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division easier. The different types of properties of whole numbers are as follows.
## Properties of Addition
## (i) Closure Property
When two numbers a and b are added, the result, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> will also be a whole number.
Therefore, whole numbers are closed for addition.
(ii) Commutative Property
If a and b are two whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. In other words, when whole numbers are added, the order does not matter. This property is called Commutative Property. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow></math>. So, whole numbers are commutative for addition.
## (iii) Associative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and c are three whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> i.e., the manner of associating numbers does not change the result. This property is called Associative Property.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math>
So, whole numbers are associative under addition.
(iv) Additive Identity
Additive Identity is a number which when added to any whole number, then the value remains the same. Let a be any whole number, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. So, 0 is the additive identity of whole numbers.
## Properties of Subtraction
(i) Closure Property
If a and b are two whole numbers such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is a whole number. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is not a whole number.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> ?
Therefore, whole numbers are not closed under subtraction.
(ii) Commutative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are two whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is not equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>9</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>≠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></math>. So, the subtraction of whole numbers is not commutative.
(iii) Associative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and c are whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is not equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## Properties of Multiplication
(i) Closure Property
If a and b are whole numbers, then their product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> will always be a whole number.
So, whole numbers are closed under multiplication.
(ii) Commutative Property
When two whole numbers, a and b are multiplied in any order, then their product remains the same. This property is called commutative property. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>
So, whole numbers are commutative under multiplication.
(iii) Associative Property
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and c are three whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></math>
So, whole numbers are associative under multiplication.
(iv) Multiplicative Identity
When any whole number a is multiplied by 1 , the product is the same number a, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>×</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. So, 1 is called the multiplicative identity in whole numbers.
(v) Multiplication By Zero
If a is any whole number, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>×</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.
(vi) Distributivity of Multiplication Over Addition or Subtraction :
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are any three whole numbers, then

For example : 6 is a perfect number as 1,2,3 and 6 are the factor of 6 and 6=1+2+3+6=12. ## EVEN AND ODD NUMBERS ## Even Numbers Numbers which are multiples of 2 are called even numbers. All the even numbers always end with 0,2,4,6, or 8 . ## Odd Numbers The numbers which are not multiples of 2 . are called odd numbers. All odd numbers end with 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 . ## PRIME AND COMPOSITE NUMBER We know that every number has at least two factors, 1 and the number itself. Only 1 is the number which has only one factor i.e. 1 . So we can divide the numbers into two groups on the basis of number of factors: ## Prime Numbers Those numbers which have exactly two factors, namely 1 and the number itself are known as prime numbers. For example: 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23 etc. are some prime numbers. ## Composite Numbers Those numbers which have more than two factors are called composite numbers. For example : 4,6,8,9,10,12,14, etc. are some composite numbers. ## Some Important Facts (i) 1 is neither prime nor composite number. (ii) 2 is the only even prime number. (iii) 2 is the smallest prime number. (iv) 4 is the smallest composite number. (v) There is no number which has no factor. ## Prime Numbers From 1 to 100 A Greek mathematician Eratosthenes found a very simple method for finding the Prime and Composite numbers in third century B.C. This method is called 'Sieve of Erastosthenes'. NOTE : A prime number (except 2) cannot have 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 at its ones place. (i) Prepare a table of natural numbers from 1 to 100. (ii) Cross out 1 as we know that it is not a prime number. (iii) Encircle the first and only even prime number i.e. 2 and cross out all its multiples as these are composite numbers. A polygon with four sides is known as quadrilateral. A quadrilateral has four vertices, four sides and two diagonals.

Two sides of a quadrilateral are called its opposite sides, if they do not have a common end point. AB and CD , AD and BC are two pairs of opposite sides of quadrilateral ABCD .

Two angles of a quadrilateral having a common side are called its adjacent angles.

Two angles of a quadrilateral which are not adjacent angles are known as opposite angles.

## Regular Polygon
A polygon is called regular if all its sides and angles are equal e.g. square, equilateral triangle, etc.
## CIRCLE
A circle is a simple closed curve, all the points of which are at the same distance from a given fixed point. They remain constant.
For example : shapes of wheels, coins etc.
## Parts of a Circle
## Centre
The fixed point in the plane which is equidistant from every point on the boundary of the circle is called centre. In the adjoining figure, O is the centre of the circle.
## Radius
The fixed distance between the centre and any point on the circle is called radius. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a radius.
## Chord
A line segment joining any two points on the circle is called a chord of the circle. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a chord.
## Diameter
A chord that passes through the centre of a circle is called diameter of the circle. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a diameter. The length of a diameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi></mrow></math> radius. In a circle, diameter is the longest chord.
## Circumference
The distance around a circle is called the circumference. Circumference of a circle is the perimeter of that circle.
## Basic Geometrical Ideas
## Arc
A part of a circumference is called an arc. In the above figure, the curve line AR is an arc of the circle. It is written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>⏜</mo></mover></mrow></math>. A chord of a circle divides it into two parts. The smaller part the minor arc and the greater part is the major arc of the circle. Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the minor arc and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the major arc.
## Segment
The region of circle enclosed by an arc and its correponding chord is called a segment.
The segment formed by a minor arc and its corresponding chord is called a minor segment.
The segment formed by a major arc and its corresponding chord is called a major segment.
## Sector
The region of circle enclosed by an arc and two radii of a circle is called sector. In the adjoining figure, shaded area covered by AOB is sector of the circle.
## Concentric circles
Two or more circles with the same centre and different radii are called concentric circles.

## Points line, ray and line segment
- A point determines a location. It does not have length, breadth and thickness. It is denoted by capital letter.
- A line segment is the shortest distance between two points.
- A line is obtained by extending line segment in both directions indefinitely.
- A ray is a portion of line starting at a point and extending in one direction endlessly.
## Polygon
- A drawing (straight or nonstraight) drawn without lifting the pencil is called a curve.
- A simple curve does not cross itself.
- If the ends of a curve are joined, then it is called a closed curve.
- If the ends of a curve are not joined, then it is called an open curve.
- A closed curve made up of line segments is called a polygon. These line segments are the sides of the polygon.

## QUADRILATERALS
A polygon with four sides is known as quadrilateral. A quadrilateral has four vertices, four sides and two diagonals.
In a quadrilateral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> and D are vertices. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and DA are sides of the quadrilateral. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> are angles of the quadrilateral. A circle is a simple closed curve, all the points of which are at the same distance from a given fixed point. They remain constant.
For example : shapes of wheels, coins etc.
## Parts of a Circle
## Centre
The fixed point in the plane which is equidistant from every point on the boundary of the circle is called centre. In the adjoining figure, O is the centre of the circle.
## Radius
The fixed distance between the centre and any point on the circle is called radius. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a radius.
## Chord
A line segment joining any two points on the circle is called a chord of the circle. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a chord.
## Diameter
A chord that passes through the centre of a circle is called diameter of the circle. In the figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> is a diameter. The length of a diameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi></mrow></math> radius. In a circle, diameter is the longest chord.
## Circumference
The distance around a circle is called the circumference. Circumference of a circle is the perimeter of that circle.

## Segment
The region of circle enclosed by an arc and its correponding chord is called a segment.
The segment formed by a minor arc and its corresponding chord is called a minor segment.
The segment formed by a major arc and its corresponding chord is called a major segment.
## Sector
The region of circle enclosed by an arc and two radii of a circle is called sector. In the adjoining figure, shaded area covered by AOB is sector of the circle.
## Concentric circles
Two or more circles with the same centre and different radii are called concentric circles.

When 0 is added to any integer, the result is the integer itself. So, 0 is called the additive identity of integers. e.g.
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>

## Additive inverse
If we add the negative of a number to the number itself, the result is 0 . The number and its negative are called the additive inverse of each other. For example:
(i) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>

In the above examples, 2 and ( -2 ), 4 and ( -4 ) are the additive inverse of each other.
NOTE : Additive inverse of 0 is 0 .

## Types of Fractions
There are different types of fractions. Let us learn about them.
## Proper fraction
A fraction whose numerator is less than its denominator is called a proper fraction. A proper fraction is always less than a whole, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## Improper fraction
A fraction whose numerator is greater than or equal to its denominator is called an improper fraction. An improper fraction is always equal to or greater than a whole, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## Unit fraction
Fractions with numerator 1 are called unit fractions, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## Mixed fraction
A combination of a whole and a proper fraction is called a mixed fraction, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.

## Representation of proper fraction
Consider various proper fractions namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>. etc.
Each of them is greater than zero but less than 1 , so each one of them lies between 0 and 1 . Now, draw a number line and mark two points on it and name them as 0 and 1 . To show <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> on number line, we divide the gap between 0 and 1 into as many parts as the denominator of the fraction i.e., 4 and move as many steps forward as the numerator of the fraction i.e., 3.

## EQUIVALENT FRACTIONS
Equivalent fractions are the fractions which represent the same value. They represent the same part of a whole. To find equivalent fractions of any given fraction :
(i) We may multiply both the numerator and the denominator of the given fraction by the same number.
(ii) We may divide both the numerator and the denominator of the given fraction by the same number.

## LIKE AND UNLIKE FRACTIONS
Fractions with same denominators are called like fractions.
For example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> are unlike fractions.
The fractions with different denominators are called unlike fractions
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>39</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>46</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> are unlike fractions.

## Comparison of unlike fractions.
Unlike fractions can be compared by any of the following two methods :
## 1. By converting them into like fractions :
To compare unlike fractions, we first convert them into like fractions by obtaining their equivalent fraction with a denominator which is LCM of the denominators of both the fractions.
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> can be compared by converting them into like fractions having their denominator equal to LCM of 5 and 7 .
L.C.M. of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mtext> and </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Now, </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## 2. Cross multiplication method :
To compare any two fractions such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, we cross multiply as shown below.
Thus, the cross products are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
(a) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo>></mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow></mrow></math> then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(b) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow></mrow></math> then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo><</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
(c) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow></mrow></math> then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
NOTE: When two fractions have same numerator, but different denominators, then the fraction with smaller denominator is greater. ## Types of Fractions
There are different types of fractions. Let us learn about them.
## Proper fraction
A fraction whose numerator is less than its denominator is called a proper fraction. A proper fraction is always less than a whole, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## Improper fraction
A fraction whose numerator is greater than or equal to its denominator is called an improper fraction. An improper fraction is always equal to or greater than a whole, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## Unit fraction
Fractions with numerator 1 are called unit fractions, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## Mixed fraction
A combination of a whole and a proper fraction is called a mixed fraction, e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> etc.
## REPRESENTATION OF FRACTION ON NUMBERS LINE
We have learnt the representation of integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>…</mi></mrow></math> etc. on number line. We will now learn the representation of fractions on number line.
## Representation of proper fraction
Consider various proper fractions namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>…</mi></mrow></math>. etc.
Each of them is greater than zero but less than 1 , so each one of them lies between 0 and 1 . Now, draw a number line and mark two points on it and name them as 0 and 1 . To show <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> on number line, we divide the gap between 0 and 1 into as many parts as the denominator of the fraction i.e., 4 and move as many steps forward as the numerator of the fraction i.e., 3.

## EQUIVALENT FRACTIONS
Equivalent fractions are the fractions which represent the same value. They represent the same part of a whole. To find equivalent fractions of any given fraction :
(i) We may multiply both the numerator and the denominator of the given fraction by the same number.
(ii) We may divide both the numerator and the denominator of the given fraction by the same number.

## COMPARISON OF FRACTIONS
## Comparison of Like Fractions
When we compare two fractions having same denominator, then the fraction with greater numerator will be greater.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## Fractions
## Comparison of unlike fractions.
Unlike fractions can be compared by any of the following two methods :
## 1. By converting them into like fractions :
To compare unlike fractions, we first convert them into like fractions by obtaining their equivalent fraction with a denominator which is LCM of the denominators of both the fractions.
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> can be compared by converting them into like fractions having their denominator equal to LCM of 5 and 7 .
L.C.M. of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mtext> and </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Now, </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## 2. Cross multiplication method :
To compare any two fractions such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>, we cross multiply as shown below.

(b) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow></mrow></math> then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo><</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## LIKE AND UNLIKE DECIMALS
The decimals having the same number of decimal places are called like decimals.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.37</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15.14</mn></mrow></math> and 13.86, are like decimals. All have two decimal places.
The decimals having different number of decimal places are called unlike decimals.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.34</mn></mrow></math> and 1.386 are unlike decimals. They have different number of decimals places.
## Conversion of unlike decimals into like decimals
To convert unlike decimals into like decimals, we put extra zeros to the extreme right of decimal part to make number of digits equal after decimal.
For example: Let us convert 7, 5.3, 9.21 and 8.406 into like decimal.
Here, the maximum number of decimal places is 3 .
Now, convert all decimals into like decimals by putting extra zeros to the extreme right of the decimal part.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7.000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5.3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5.300</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9.21</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9.210</mn></mrow></math>
NOTE: Adding extra zeros to the right of a decimal does not change its value i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.96</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.96000</mn></mrow></math>
## COMPARISON OF DECIMALS
To compare two decimals we should follow the following steps:
Step 1 : Compare the whole number part, the decimals having greater whole part is greater.
Step 2 : If the whole number parts are equal, then compare the tenth digits. The decimal number with greater tenth digit is greater.
Step 3 : If the tenths digit are equal, then compare the hundredths digit. The decimal number having greater hundredths digit is greater and so on.
For example: Let us compare 4.397 and 4.391
Compare the whole parts of both the numbers. But, whole parts are same.
Now, compare tenths digits. But tenths are also same.
So, compare hundredths digits. These are also same.
Now, compare thousandths digits. Clearly, 7 thousandths <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> thousandth
So, 4.397 > 4.391

## Decimals

## LIKE AND UNLIKE DECIMALS
The decimals having the same number of decimal places are called like decimals.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.37</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15.14</mn></mrow></math> and 13.86, are like decimals. All have two decimal places.
The decimals having different number of decimal places are called unlike decimals.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>0.6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.34</mn></mrow></math> and 1.386 are unlike decimals. They have different number of decimals places.
## Conversion of unlike decimals into like decimals
To convert unlike decimals into like decimals, we put extra zeros to the extreme right of decimal part to make number of digits equal after decimal.
For example: Let us convert 7, 5.3, 9.21 and 8.406 into like decimal.
Here, the maximum number of decimal places is 3 .
Now, convert all decimals into like decimals by putting extra zeros to the extreme right of the decimal part.

## COMPARISON OF DECIMALS
To compare two decimals we should follow the following steps:
Step 1 : Compare the whole number part, the decimals having greater whole part is greater.
Step 2 : If the whole number parts are equal, then compare the tenth digits. The decimal number with greater tenth digit is greater.
Step 3 : If the tenths digit are equal, then compare the hundredths digit. The decimal number having greater hundredths digit is greater and so on.
For example: Let us compare 4.397 and 4.391
Compare the whole parts of both the numbers. But, whole parts are same.
Now, compare tenths digits. But tenths are also same.
So, compare hundredths digits. These are also same.
Now, compare thousandths digits. Clearly, 7 thousandths <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> thousandth
So, 4.397 > 4.391

By observing a bar graph we can understand what kind of data it represents and draw certain conclusions from it. This is known as interpretation of the bar graph.

We can find the area of regular and irregular figures by using a graph or squared paper. To find the area, first we draw the figure on the graph paper covering as many squares as possible.

(i) Count the number of complete squares of unit length enclosed by the figure.

We can find the area of regular and irregular figures by using a graph or squared paper. To find the area, first we draw the figure on the graph paper covering as many squares as possible.
For finding the area by using squared paper, we have to follow the following steps :
(i) Count the number of complete squares of unit length enclosed by the figure.
(ii) Count the number of those squares whose more than half parts are enclosed by the figure.
(iii) Count the number of those squares whose exact half parts are enclosed by the figure and divide the number by 2 .
(iv) Leave those squares whose less than half parts are enclosed by the figure.
(v) Add all the steps (i), (ii), and (iii) to obtain the area.

## PROPORTION
Proportion is defined as an equality of two ratios,
Four (non-zero) quantities of the same kind <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and d are said to be in proportion if the ratio of a to b is equal to the ratio of c to d
i.e., if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
We can write as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> are in proportion and are respectively known as first, second, third and fourth term of the given proportion.
Here, the 1st and 4th terms are called the extreme terms or extremes. The 2nd and 3rd terms are called the middle terms or means. We can also say, in proportion, Product of extremes = Product of means
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> are in proportion then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>
i.e. Product of extremes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Product of means
ILLUSTRATIOM : 9
Are the numbers 40, 30, 60 and 45 in proportion?
Given terms are 40, 30, 60 and 45
Product of extremes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1800</mn></mrow></math>
Product of means <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1800</mn></mrow></math>
Product of extremes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Product of means

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>18</mn><mi>:</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>:</mi><mn>27</mn><mi>:</mi><mn>36</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mi>x</mi><mi>×</mi><mn>27</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>36</mn><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>18</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>36</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>27</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>.</mo></mrow></math>

## PROPORTION
Proportion is defined as an equality of two ratios,
Four (non-zero) quantities of the same kind <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> and d are said to be in proportion if the ratio of a to b is equal to the ratio of c to d
i.e., if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
We can write as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>:</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>
Here, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> are in proportion and are respectively known as first, second, third and fourth term of the given proportion.
Here, the 1st and 4th terms are called the extreme terms or extremes. The 2nd and 3rd terms are called the middle terms or means. We can also say, in proportion, Product of extremes = Product of means
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> are in proportion then,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>×</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>
i.e. Product of extremes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Product of means
ILLUSTRATIOM : 9
Are the numbers 40, 30, 60 and 45 in proportion?
Given terms are 40, 30, 60 and 45
Product of extremes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1800</mn></mrow></math>
Product of means <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1800</mn></mrow></math>
Product of extremes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> Product of means
Thus 40, 30, 60 and 45 are in proportion.
## Alternate method:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mtext> Ratio of </mtext><mn>40</mn><mtext> to </mtext><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>40</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>;</mi><mtext> Ratio of </mtext><mn>60</mn><mtext> to </mtext><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>60</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>45</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
Both the ratios are equal. Therefore the numbers are in proportion.

## LIKE AND UNLIKE FRACTIONS
Fractions with same denominators are called like fractions.
## For example :
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>17</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>31</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> are unlike fractions.
The fractions with different denominators are called unlike fractions
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>13</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>39</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>46</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> are unlike fractions.
## COMPARISON OF FRACTIONS
## Comparison of Like Fractions
When we compare two fractions having same denominator, then the fraction with greater numerator will be greater.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## Comparison of unlike fractions.
Unlike fractions can be compared by any of the following two methods :
## 1. By converting them into like fractions:
To compare unlike fractions, we first convert them into like fractions by obtaining their equivalent fraction with a denominator which is LCM of the denominators of both the fractions.
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> can be compared by converting them into like fractions having their denominator equal to LCM of 5 and 7 .
L.C.M. of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mtext> and </mtext><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mtext> Now, </mtext><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>21</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>35</mn></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## 2. Cross multiplication method :

(b) If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo><</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow></mrow></math> then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo><</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>×</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>9</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>

## Division of whole number by a fraction

For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>÷</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow></math>
For dividing a whole number by a mixed fraction, first convert the mixed fraction into improper fraction and then divide
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>15</mn><mi>÷</mi><mn>3</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mi>÷</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mi>×</mi><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>30</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## DECIMALS
Numbers in form of 1.18, 22.36, 853.4448 are known as decimal numbers.
A decimal number have two parts. A whole number part and decimal number part. These two parts are separated by a dot. This dot is known as decimal point. The whole number part is in the left of the decimal point and the decimal part to the right of decimal point.
Thus, in 63.825
The number of digits contained in the decimal part shows its decimal places.
For example: 6.438 have three digits in decimal part which is known as three decimal places.
## Like and Unlike Decimlas
Decimals having the same number of decimal places are called like decimals.
For example: 6.238, 38.937, 48.385 are like decimals.
Decimals having different number of decimal places are called unlike decimals.
For example: 6.238, 32.73, 65.3984 are unlike decimals.
NOTE: On adding zeros after the last digit of the decimal part of any decimal number does not change the value of the decimal.
For example: 6.28 can be 6.280 or 6.2800 but the value of all three are same.
We use this property to convert the unlike decimal into like decimal.
## Comparing decimals:
To compare two given decimals, We have the following steps:
1. Convert the given decimals into like decimals.
2. First compare the whole number part. The decimal with greater whole number part is greater.
3. If the whole-number parts are equal, compare the tenths digits. The decimal with bigger digit in tenths place is greater.
4. If the tenths digits are also equal, compare the hundreths digits, and so on.

## Comparison of Like Fractions
When we compare two fractions having same denominator, then the fraction with greater numerator will be greater.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>></mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
## Comparison of unlike fractions.
Unlike fractions can be compared by any of the following two methods :
## 1. By converting them into like fractions:
To compare unlike fractions, we first convert them into like fractions by obtaining their equivalent fraction with a denominator which is LCM of the denominators of both the fractions.
e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> can be compared by converting them into like fractions having their denominator equal to LCM of 5 and 7 .

## DECIMALS
Numbers in form of 1.18, 22.36, 853.4448 are known as decimal numbers.
A decimal number have two parts. A whole number part and decimal number part. These two parts are separated by a dot. This dot is known as decimal point. The whole number part is in the left of the decimal point and the decimal part to the right of decimal point.
Thus, in 63.825
The number of digits contained in the decimal part shows its decimal places.
For example: 6.438 have three digits in decimal part which is known as three decimal places.
## Like and Unlike Decimlas
Decimals having the same number of decimal places are called like decimals.
For example: 6.238, 38.937, 48.385 are like decimals.
Decimals having different number of decimal places are called unlike decimals.
For example: 6.238, 32.73, 65.3984 are unlike decimals.
NOTE: On adding zeros after the last digit of the decimal part of any decimal number does not change the value of the decimal.
For example: 6.28 can be 6.280 or 6.2800 but the value of all three are same.
We use this property to convert the unlike decimal into like decimal.
## Comparing decimals:
To compare two given decimals, We have the following steps:
1. Convert the given decimals into like decimals.
2. First compare the whole number part. The decimal with greater whole number part is greater.
3. If the whole-number parts are equal, compare the tenths digits. The decimal with bigger digit in tenths place is greater.
4. If the tenths digits are also equal, compare the hundreths digits, and so on.

## ANGLES FORMED BY A TRANSVERSAL
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are two lines cut by a transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. The transversal makes eight angles, which are marked as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> and 8 in the following figure.
## (i) Exterior angles
Exterior angles are the angles that lie outside the lines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, cut by a transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. In the above figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> are the exterior angles.
## (ii) Interior angles
Those angles which lie between the two lines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, are interior angles. In other words, interior angles are the angles that are formed by two lines cut by a transversal and are between the two lines.
In the above figure; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> are the interior angles.
## (iii) Corresponding Angles
The pair of angles, one of which is an exterior angle while other is interior angle, that are on the same side of transversal, are corresponding angles. These angles are non-adjacent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ) are corresponding angles.
## (iv) Alternate Interior angles
Alternate interior angles are non-adjacent interior angles that lie on opposite sides of transversal. ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ) and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ) are alternate interior angles.
## (v) Alternate Exterior Angles
Alternate interior angles are non-adjacent exterior angles that lie on opposite sides of transversal. ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ) and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ) are alternate exterior angles.
## Consecutive Interior Angles
Consecutive Interior Angles are pairs of interior angles that are on the same side of the transversal. These angles are commonly known as Co-interior angles.
In the above figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are co-interior angles.

## PROPERTIES OF ANGLES FORMED WHEN A TRANSVERSAL CUTS TWO PARALLEL LINES
## Angles Formed when a Transversal Cuts Two Parallel Lines
Let two parallel lines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> be cut by a transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, forming angles as shown, we have:
(i) Corresponding angles: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are called pairs of corresponding angles. Angles in each pair are equal to each other i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>

Angles in each pair are equal to each other.
That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math>.

Angles in each pair are equal to each other. That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>.

That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

Two lines that are cut by a transversal are parallel if :

- alternate exterior angles are equal or
- corresponding angles are equal or

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> are two lines cut by a transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. The transversal makes eight angles, which are marked as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> and 8 in the following figure.
## (i) Exterior angles
Exterior angles are the angles that lie outside the lines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, cut by a transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. In the above figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> are the exterior angles.
## (ii) Interior angles
Those angles which lie between the two lines <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, are interior angles. In other words, interior angles are the angles that are formed by two lines cut by a transversal and are between the two lines.
In the above figure; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> are the interior angles.
## (iii) Corresponding Angles
The pair of angles, one of which is an exterior angle while other is interior angle, that are on the same side of transversal, are corresponding angles. These angles are non-adjacent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ) are corresponding angles.
## (iv) Alternate Interior angles
Alternate interior angles are non-adjacent interior angles that lie on opposite sides of transversal. ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> ) and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></math> ) are alternate interior angles.
## (v) Alternate Exterior Angles
Alternate interior angles are non-adjacent exterior angles that lie on opposite sides of transversal. ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ) and ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> ) are alternate exterior angles.
## Consecutive Interior Angles
Consecutive Interior Angles are pairs of interior angles that are on the same side of the transversal. These angles are commonly known as Co-interior angles.
In the above figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are co-interior angles.

## Test for parallel lines
The properties of parallel lines can be used to find whether given lines are parallel or not parallel.

- alternate interior angles are equal or
- alternate exterior angles are equal or
- corresponding angles are equal or

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

3. Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 8 cm long. What can be the length of its third side?
Sol. Let the length of the third side be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. We know that the sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mi>x</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math>.
Also, we know that the difference of any two sides of a triangle is less than the third side.
## AMPLES
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>⇒</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.
Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow></math>.
Hence, the length of the third side must be greater than 2 cm and smaller than 14 cm .
