Sol. It is given that in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow></mrow><mo accent="true">―</mo></mover></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>35</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>35</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo></mrow></math> base angles are equal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math>
So, the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is an isosceles triangle.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>35</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>35</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>110</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>110</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mspace width="1em" /><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>∵</mo></mrow></math> in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math> base angles are equal]
Now in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>70</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>40</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
Hence, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, i.e., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>40</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.
5. A ladder is placed in such a way that its foot is at a distance of 5 m from a wall and its top reaches a window 12 m above the ground. Determine the length of the ladder.
Sol. Let AB be the ladder and B be the window.
Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> is a right-angled triangle at C .
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>12</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>169</mn></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>⇒</mo><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>169</mn></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Hence, the length of the ladder is 13 m .
6. The sides of certain triangles are given below.
Determine which of them are right triangles:

(ii) Here, the larger side is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. 7. A man drives 3 km towards north and then 4 km towards east. How far is he away from his initial position?
Sol. Let the starting point be A and final point is C as shown in the figure.

The word 'per cent' is an abbreviation of the Latin phrase 'per centum' which means per hundred or hundredths.

The word 'per cent' is an abbreviation of the Latin phrase 'per centum' which means per hundred or hundredths.

## TRIANGLE AS PARTS OF RECTANGLES
The diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two equal triangle. Thus, the sum of the areas of the two triangles is the same as the area of the rectangle.
For example: PQRS is a rectangle.
PR divides the rectangle into two triangles; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.

## Generalising for other Congruent Parts of Rectangles
When a rectangle is divided into two equal parts, such that one part is congruent or superpose on the other part, then the area of one part is equal to the area of the other part.

## LAWS OF EXPONENTS
## Law 1 : Multiplying powers with the same base
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is any non-zero rational number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
i.e. in case of multiplication, if base are same, simply add the powers.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
## Law 2 : Finding quotients of powers of the same number
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is any non-zero rational number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mi>÷</mi><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> i.e. for division with same bases, subtract the exponents.
For example : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mi>÷</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>

## Law 3 : Finding a power of a power of a rational number
For any non-zero rational number, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> i.e. to find a power of a power of a number, we multiply the exponents.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mspace linebreak="newline" /><mi>&</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="prefix">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true" fence="true" form="postfix">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mn>15</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></math>

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are two non-zero rational numbers and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is a whole number, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

i.e. in case of multiplication, if base are same, simply add the powers.
For example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mspace width="1em" /><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mi>×</mi><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>×</mi><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is any non-zero rational number and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> are whole numbers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mi>÷</mi><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> i.e. for division with same bases, subtract the exponents.

## Rules for Solving a Linear Equation in One Variable
While solving a linear equation, following rules are to be remembered.
(a) Addition/ subtraction of same quantity to/from both sides of an equation does not change the equality
(b) Multiplication by a same number on both sides of an equation does not change the equality
(c) Division by a same non-zero number on both sides of an equation does not change the equality.
(d) Any term may be transposed from one side of equality to another side by changing the sign of the term (from + to - , or from to + ),
(e) A multiplier may be removed from one side of an equation by making it a divisor on the other side.
(f) A divisor may be removed from one side of an equation by making it a multiplier on the other side.

## CROSS-MULTIPLICATION METHOD
Let equation be of the form : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
Consider the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
Equation is obtained directly by equating the product of numerator of L.H.S. and denominator of R.H.S. to the product of denominator of L.H.S. and numerator of R.H.S.
This can be exhibited as follows: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
This process of multiplying the mumerator of L.H.S. with the denominator on R.H.S. and equating it to the product of the denominator on L.H.S. with the numerator on R.H.S. is called cross-multiplication.
So, we can convert an equation of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> to a linear equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## DIFFERENT TYPES OF QUADRILATERALS
## Trapezium
A quadrilateral in which one pair of opposite sides is parallel and the other pair of sides is non-parallel and not equal is called trapezium. In the given figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a trapezium in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> whereas <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> are its non-parallel sides.
## Isosceles Trapezium
If the non-parallel sides of the trapezium ( AD and BC as shown in figure) are equal, then it is called an isoceles trapezium. In the trapezium <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>; AD and BC are its non-parellel sides such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. So, ABCD is an isosceles trapezium. In an isosceles trapezium, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
Isosceles Trapezium
NOTE: Non-parallel sides of a trapezium are called lateral sides.
## Kite
A quadrilateral in which two pairs opf adjacent sides are equal is called a kite. It has uequal opposite sides.
In the adjoining figure, ABCD is a kite.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Diagonals AC and BD intersect each other at right angles.
## Parallelogram
A quadrilateral with both pair of opposite sides parallel is called a parallelogram.
In the adjoining figure <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Thus, ABCD is a parallelogram.
Sides of Parallelogram
The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
Consider a parallelogram ABCD .
Join the diagonal AC .
In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, alternate interior angles).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (common),
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, alternate interior angles).
By ASA congruency rule, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
By c.p.c.t.s., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Thus, pair of opposite sides are equal.
## Angles of Parallelogram
## Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
Let us consider a parallelogram ABCD in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and AD is a transversal
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
[Sum of the measures of interior angles on the same side of a transversal is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ]
Again, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and AB is a transversal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
From (i) and (ii), we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
Similarly, we can prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
Thus, the adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary and the opposite angles are equal.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## Diagonals of a Parallelogram
The diagonals of parallelogram bisect each other.
Let the diagonals of parallelogram ABCD intersect at O .
In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> [alternate interior angles].
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> [opposite sides of a parallelogram].
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> [alternative interior angles].
? By ASA congruency rule,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (c.p.c.t.s.)
Therefore, diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

But in Mathematics, we have methods for calculating the degree of certainty of an event in numerical value under certain conditions. ## Some Basic Terms Random Experiments : An experiment whose outcome has to be among a set of events that are completely known but whose exact outcome is unknown is called a random experiment, e.g. throwing of a dice, tossing of a coin. etc. Sample Space : It is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. e.g. when a coin is tossed. Sample space is (Head, Tail). Sample space when a dice is thrown is {1,2,3,4,5,6} Event : The set representing the desired outcome of a random experiment is called the event, e.g. getting head in a toss of coin is an event. Trial : Performing an experiment once is called a trial. Equally Likely Events: The results of a random experiment are said to be equally likely if the different outcomes have the same or equal chances of occurrence. For example, when a dice is thrown, each of the faces having 1,2,3,4,5 or 6 numbers are equally likely to appear. Once the event : getting a head and the event : setting a tail are mutually exclusive events. Favourable Outcome(s) : The outcome(s) which ensure the occurrence of an event are called favourable outcome(s) to that event. ## PROFIT AND LOSS
Business transactions have become common feature of daily life. When we purchase and sale some items, we either make profit or loss. Profit and loss are part of every business transactions. Let us first investigate them.
Cost Price : The Price at which a person buys an item is the Cost Price (C.P.) of that item. In other words, amount paid or expenses in purchasing or producing an item is called its cost price (C.P.).
Selling Price : The Price at which a person sells an item is the selling price(S.P.) of item. In other words, amount received when an item sold is called selling price (S.P.) of that item to the seller.
Overheads : All the expenses that a buyer paid on transportation or repair of purchased item are called overheads. All over heads are added to basic Cost Price (C.P.) of that item.
Profit : When a person sells an item at a price which is more than its cost price we say that person has made a profit or gain. The difference (S.P-C.P) is called profit or gain.
Thus Profit or Gain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> S.P - C.P, if S.P <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> C.P.
Loss : When a person sells an item at a price which is less than its cost price, we say that the person has suffered loss. The difference (C.P-S.P) is called loss.
Thus Loss <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> C.P - S.P, if S.P < C.P.

NOTE: The main difference between the simple interest and the compound interest is that the principal in the case of simple interest remains constant throughout the loan period where as in the case of compound interest, the principal changes periodically (i.e. after each conversion period) throughout the loan period.

## Inverse Variation
An inverse variation is indicated when two quantities are so related that
(i) an increase in one causes a corresponding decrease in the other or vice versa and
(ii) the ratio of any two values of one quantity is the inverse of the ratio of the corresponding values of the other.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> are variables, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> varies inversely as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∝</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is constant of proportionality, Also <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>

## Rules for Solving a Linear Equation in One Variable
While solving a linear equation, following rules are to be remembered.
(a) Addition/ subtraction of same quantity to/from both sides of an equation does not change the equality
(b) Multiplication by a same number on both sides of an equation does not change the equality
(c) Division by a same non-zero number on both sides of an equation does not change the equality.
(d) Any term may be transposed from one side of equality to another side by changing the sign of the term (from + to - , or from to + ),
(e) A multiplier may be removed from one side of an equation by making it a divisor on the other side.
(f) A divisor may be removed from one side of an equation by making it a multiplier on the other side.

## CROSS-MULTIPLICATION METHOD
Let equation be of the form : <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.
Consider the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext> </mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>.
Equation is obtained directly by equating the product of numerator of L.H.S. and denominator of R.H.S. to the product of denominator of L.H.S. and numerator of R.H.S.
This can be exhibited as follows: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
This process of multiplying the mumerator of L.H.S. with the denominator on R.H.S. and equating it to the product of the denominator on L.H.S. with the numerator on R.H.S. is called cross-multiplication.
So, we can convert an equation of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> to a linear equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

## DIFFERENT TYPES OF QUADRILATERALS
## Trapezium
A quadrilateral in which one pair of opposite sides is parallel and the other pair of sides is non-parallel and not equal is called trapezium. In the given figure, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is a trapezium in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> whereas <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> are its non-parallel sides.
## Isosceles Trapezium
If the non-parallel sides of the trapezium ( AD and BC as shown in figure) are equal, then it is called an isoceles trapezium. In the trapezium <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>; AD and BC are its non-parellel sides such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>. So, ABCD is an isosceles trapezium. In an isosceles trapezium, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>.
Isosceles Trapezium
NOTE: Non-parallel sides of a trapezium are called lateral sides.
## Kite
A quadrilateral in which two pairs opf adjacent sides are equal is called a kite. It has uequal opposite sides.
In the adjoining figure, ABCD is a kite.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Diagonals AC and BD intersect each other at right angles.
## Parallelogram
A quadrilateral with both pair of opposite sides parallel is called a parallelogram.
In the adjoining figure <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Thus, ABCD is a parallelogram.
Sides of Parallelogram
The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
Consider a parallelogram ABCD .
Join the diagonal AC .
In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, alternate interior angles).
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (common),
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> ( <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>, alternate interior angles).
By ASA congruency rule, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
By c.p.c.t.s., <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Thus, pair of opposite sides are equal.
## Angles of Parallelogram
## Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
Let us consider a parallelogram ABCD in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>.
Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and AD is a transversal
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
[Sum of the measures of interior angles on the same side of a transversal is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ]
Again, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and AB is a transversal.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>
From (i) and (ii), we have
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><mspace width="1em" /><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>
Similarly, we can prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>.
Thus, the adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary and the opposite angles are equal.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∴</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>⇒</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mrow><mo>∘</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>

## Diagonals of a Parallelogram
The diagonals of parallelogram bisect each other.
Let the diagonals of parallelogram ABCD intersect at O .
In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> [alternate interior angles].
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> [opposite sides of a parallelogram].
and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>∠</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mn>4</mn><mspace width="1em" /></mrow></math> [alternative interior angles].
? By ASA congruency rule,
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>Δ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>≅</mo><mi>△</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math>
Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></mrow></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">D</mi></mrow></mrow></math> (c.p.c.t.s.)
Therefore, diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

But in Mathematics, we have methods for calculating the degree of certainty of an event in numerical value under certain conditions. ## Some Basic Terms Random Experiments : An experiment whose outcome has to be among a set of events that are completely known but whose exact outcome is unknown is called a random experiment, e.g. throwing of a dice, tossing of a coin. etc. Sample Space : It is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. e.g. when a coin is tossed. Sample space is (Head, Tail). Sample space when a dice is thrown is {1,2,3,4,5,6} Event : The set representing the desired outcome of a random experiment is called the event, e.g. getting head in a toss of coin is an event. Trial : Performing an experiment once is called a trial. Equally Likely Events: The results of a random experiment are said to be equally likely if the different outcomes have the same or equal chances of occurrence. For example, when a dice is thrown, each of the faces having 1,2,3,4,5 or 6 numbers are equally likely to appear. Once the event : getting a head and the event : setting a tail are mutually exclusive events. Favourable Outcome(s) : The outcome(s) which ensure the occurrence of an event are called favourable outcome(s) to that event. ## PROFIT AND LOSS
Business transactions have become common feature of daily life. When we purchase and sale some items, we either make profit or loss. Profit and loss are part of every business transactions. Let us first investigate them.
Cost Price : The Price at which a person buys an item is the Cost Price (C.P.) of that item. In other words, amount paid or expenses in purchasing or producing an item is called its cost price (C.P.).
Selling Price : The Price at which a person sells an item is the selling price(S.P.) of item. In other words, amount received when an item sold is called selling price (S.P.) of that item to the seller.
Overheads : All the expenses that a buyer paid on transportation or repair of purchased item are called overheads. All over heads are added to basic Cost Price (C.P.) of that item.
Profit : When a person sells an item at a price which is more than its cost price we say that person has made a profit or gain. The difference (S.P-C.P) is called profit or gain.
Thus Profit or Gain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> S.P - C.P, if S.P <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow></math> C.P.
Loss : When a person sells an item at a price which is less than its cost price, we say that the person has suffered loss. The difference (C.P-S.P) is called loss.
Thus Loss <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> C.P - S.P, if S.P < C.P.

NOTE: The main difference between the simple interest and the compound interest is that the principal in the case of simple interest remains constant throughout the loan period where as in the case of compound interest, the principal changes periodically (i.e. after each conversion period) throughout the loan period.

## Inverse Variation
An inverse variation is indicated when two quantities are so related that
(i) an increase in one causes a corresponding decrease in the other or vice versa and
(ii) the ratio of any two values of one quantity is the inverse of the ratio of the corresponding values of the other.
If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> are variables, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> varies inversely as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∝</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is constant of proportionality, Also <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>

## ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE
The Greek scientist Archimedes' established a relationship between buoyancy and displaced liquid in the third century BC. It is stated as follows: when an object is partially or wholly immersed in a fluid, it loses some of its weight which is equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.
It applies to both liquids and gases. If an immersed object displaces 1 kg of fluid, the buoyant force acting on it is equal to the weight of 1 kg of the fluid.
Notice that unless the container is compressed, the buoyant force is equal to the weight of the displaced liquid at any depth, as long as it is completely submerged. This is because, at any depth, it can displace no greater volume of the liquid than its own volume.
## Archimedes' (287-212 BC) and the Gold Crown
According to popular legend, Archimedes' had been given the task of determining whether a crown made for King Hiero II of Syracuse was of pure gold or whether it contained some less expensive metals, such as silver. Archimedes' problem was to find the density of the crown without destroying it. He could weigh the gold, but determining its volume was a problem. The story has it that Archimedes' came to the solution when he noted the rise in water level while immersing his body in the public baths of Syracuse. Legend reports that he excitedly rushed naked through the streets shouting "Eureka! Eureka!" ("I have found it! I have found it!").
What Archimedes' had discovered was a simple and accurate method of finding the volume of an irregular object - the displacement method of determining volumes. Once he knew both the weight and volume, he could calculate the density. Then the density of the crown could be compared to the density of gold. Archimedes' insight preceded Newton's laws of motion, from which Archimedes' principle can be derived, by almost 2000 years.
```
If the weight of a body submerged in a liquid is more than the weight of the liquid displaced,
the body will sink in it.
If the weight of a body submerged in a liquid is equal or less than the weight of the liquid
displaced, the body will float.
Only in the special case of floating does the buoyant force acting on an object equal the
object's weight.
For a floating body, the weight of the body is balanced by the upthrust.
```

## FLOATATION
Iron is much denser than water and therefore iron needle sinks, but an iron ship floats. Why is this so? Consider a solid 1-ton block of iron. Iron is nearly eight times as dense as water. When it is submerged, it will displace only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ton of water, which is certainly not enough to prevent it from sinking. Suppose that we reshape the same iron block into a bowl, as shown in Figure. Although its surface area is increased, it still weighs 1 ton. When settling in water, it displaces a greater volume of water than before. The deeper it is immersed, the more water it displaces and the greater the buoyant force acting upon it. When the buoyant force equals 1 ton, it will sink no further.

When the iron boat displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight, it floats. This is called the principle of flotation.
Every ship, submarine, and dirigible must be designed to displace a weight of fluid equal to its own weight. Thus, a 10,000 ton ship must be built wide enough to displace 10,000 tons of water before it sinks too deep in the water. The same applies to vessels in the air. A dirigible or a huge balloon that weighs 100 tons displaces at least 100 tons of air. If it displaces more, it rises; if it displaces less, it descends. If it displaces exactly its weight, it hovers at a constant altitude.
Since the buoyant force upon a body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces, denser fluids will exert a greater buoyant force upon a body than less dense fluids of the same volume. A ship, therefore, floats higher in salt water than in fresh water because salt water is slightly denser than fresh water. In the same way, a solid chunk of iron will float in mercury even though it sinks in water.

## Buoyancy in a Gas
Buoyancy in gas acts in the same way as that in a liquid. Objects in a liquid are buoyed upward because the pressure acting up against the bottom of the object exceeds the pressure acting down against the top. Likewise air pressure acting up against an object immersed in air is greater than the pressure above pushing down. The buoyancy in both cases is numerically equal to the weight of fluid displaced. Archimedes' principle applies to air just as it does for liquid: When an object is wholly or partially immersed in a gas, it loses some of its weight which is equal to the weight of the displaced gas.

2. How does buoyancy change as a helium filled balloon ascends?
1. There is a buoyant force acting on you, and you are buoyed upward by it. You aren't aware of it only because your weight is so much greater.
2. If the balloon is free to expand as it rises, the increase in volume is counteracted by a decrease in the density of higher- altitude air. So, interestingly, the greater volume of displaced air doesn't weigh more, and buoyancy stays the same. If a balloon is not free to expand, buoyancy will decrease as the balloon rises because of the lesser density of the displaced air. Usually, balloons initially expand when they rise, and, if they don't eventually rupture, fabric stretching reaches a maximum and the balloons settle where buoyancy matches their weight.

## ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE
The Greek scientist Archimedes' established a relationship between buoyancy and displaced liquid in the third century BC. It is stated as follows: when an object is partially or wholly immersed in a fluid, it loses some of its weight which is equal to the weight of the displaced fluid.
It applies to both liquids and gases. If an immersed object displaces 1 kg of fluid, the buoyant force acting on it is equal to the weight of 1 kg of the fluid.
Notice that unless the container is compressed, the buoyant force is equal to the weight of the displaced liquid at any depth, as long as it is completely submerged. This is because, at any depth, it can displace no greater volume of the liquid than its own volume.
## Archimedes' (287-212 BC) and the Gold Crown
According to popular legend, Archimedes' had been given the task of determining whether a crown made for King Hiero II of Syracuse was of pure gold or whether it contained some less expensive metals, such as silver. Archimedes' problem was to find the density of the crown without destroying it. He could weigh the gold, but determining its volume was a problem. The story has it that Archimedes' came to the solution when he noted the rise in water level while immersing his body in the public baths of Syracuse. Legend reports that he excitedly rushed naked through the streets shouting "Eureka! Eureka!" ("I have found it! I have found it!").
What Archimedes' had discovered was a simple and accurate method of finding the volume of an irregular object - the displacement method of determining volumes. Once he knew both the weight and volume, he could calculate the density. Then the density of the crown could be compared to the density of gold. Archimedes' insight preceded Newton's laws of motion, from which Archimedes' principle can be derived, by almost 2000 years.
```
If the weight of a body submerged in a liquid is more than the weight of the liquid displaced,
the body will sink in it.
If the weight of a body submerged in a liquid is equal or less than the weight of the liquid
displaced, the body will float.
Only in the special case of floating does the buoyant force acting on an object equal the
object's weight.
For a floating body, the weight of the body is balanced by the upthrust.
```

## FLOATATION
Iron is much denser than water and therefore iron needle sinks, but an iron ship floats. Why is this so? Consider a solid 1-ton block of iron. Iron is nearly eight times as dense as water. When it is submerged, it will displace only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> ton of water, which is certainly not enough to prevent it from sinking. Suppose that we reshape the same iron block into a bowl, as shown in Figure. Although its surface area is increased, it still weighs 1 ton. When settling in water, it displaces a greater volume of water than before. The deeper it is immersed, the more water it displaces and the greater the buoyant force acting upon it. When the buoyant force equals 1 ton, it will sink no further.

When the iron boat displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight, it floats. This is called the principle of flotation.
Every ship, submarine, and dirigible must be designed to displace a weight of fluid equal to its own weight. Thus, a 10,000 ton ship must be built wide enough to displace 10,000 tons of water before it sinks too deep in the water. The same applies to vessels in the air. A dirigible or a huge balloon that weighs 100 tons displaces at least 100 tons of air. If it displaces more, it rises; if it displaces less, it descends. If it displaces exactly its weight, it hovers at a constant altitude.
Since the buoyant force upon a body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces, denser fluids will exert a greater buoyant force upon a body than less dense fluids of the same volume. A ship, therefore, floats higher in salt water than in fresh water because salt water is slightly denser than fresh water. In the same way, a solid chunk of iron will float in mercury even though it sinks in water.

## Buoyancy in a Gas
Buoyancy in gas acts in the same way as that in a liquid. Objects in a liquid are buoyed upward because the pressure acting up against the bottom of the object exceeds the pressure acting down against the top. Likewise air pressure acting up against an object immersed in air is greater than the pressure above pushing down. The buoyancy in both cases is numerically equal to the weight of fluid displaced. Archimedes' principle applies to air just as it does for liquid: When an object is wholly or partially immersed in a gas, it loses some of its weight which is equal to the weight of the displaced gas.
## CHECK P oint
1. Is there a buoyant force acting on you? If there is, why are you not buoyed up by this force?
2. How does buoyancy change as a helium filled balloon ascends?
1. There is a buoyant force acting on you, and you are buoyed upward by it. You aren't aware of it only because your weight is so much greater.
2. If the balloon is free to expand as it rises, the increase in volume is counteracted by a decrease in the density of higher- altitude air. So, interestingly, the greater volume of displaced air doesn't weigh more, and buoyancy stays the same. If a balloon is not free to expand, buoyancy will decrease as the balloon rises because of the lesser density of the displaced air. Usually, balloons initially expand when they rise, and, if they don't eventually rupture, fabric stretching reaches a maximum and the balloons settle where buoyancy matches their weight.

## FRICTION : A NECESSARY EVIL
Friction has advantages as well as disadvantages. In other words, friction is not desirable but without friction, we cannot think of survival, so we can say that "friction is a necessary evil". In some cases friction acts as a supporting force i.e., as a friend and in some cases it acts as opposing force i.e., as a foe.
## Friction as a Friend / Advantages of Friction :
(i) The force of friction helps us to move on the surface of earth. In the absence of friction, we cannot think of walking on the surface.
(ii) The force of friction between the tip of a pen and the surface of paper helps us to write on the paper. It is not possible to write on the glazed paper as there is no force of friction.
(iii) The force of friction between the tyres of a vehicle and the road helps the vehicle to stop when brake is applied. In the absence of friction, the vehicle skid off the road when brake is applied.
(iv) Moving belts remain on the rim of a wheel because of friction.
(v) The force of friction between a chalk and the blackboard helps us to write on the board.
Fig. 2.8
## Friction as a Foe / Disadvantages of Friction :
(i) A significant amount of energy of a moving object is wasted in the form of heat energy to overcome the force of friction.
(ii) The force of friction restricts the speed of moving vehicles like buses, trains, aeroplanes, rockets etc.
(iii) The efficiency of machines decreases due to the presence of force of friction.
(iv) The force of friction causes lot of wear and tear in the moving parts of a machine.
(v) Sometimes, a machine gets burnt due to the force of friction between different moving parts.

## INCREASING AND REDUCING FRICTION
## Methods of Increasing Friction
- Treading of tyres is done to increase friction between the road and the tyres. Moreover, synthetic rubber is preferred over the natural rubber in the manufacture of tyres because of its larger coefficient of friction with the road.
- Sand is thrown on tracks covered with snow. This increases the force of friction between the wheels and the track and the driving becomes safer.
- On a rainy day, we throw some sand on the slippery ground. This increases the friction between our feet and the ground. This reduces the chances of slipping.
## Methods of Reducing Friction
Friction can be reduced by
- polishing the surface. (but extra polishing increase friction)
- lubrication
- proper selection of material
- avoiding moisture
- streamlining the shape
- using ball bearings or roller bearings
Friction can be considerably reduced by maintaining a thin cushion of compressed air between solid surfaces in relative motion
## Wheel Reduce Friction
When objects such as a wheel (disc or ring), sphere or a cylinder rolls over a surface, the force of friction that comes into play is called rolling friction.
- Rolling friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction ( R ) and inversely proportional to the radius ( r ) of the rolling cylinder or wheel.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mtext>rolling </mtext></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is called coefficient of rolling friction, it would be measured in metre.
- Rolling friction is often quite small as compared to the sliding friction. That is why heavy loads are transported by placing them on carts with wheels.
The velocity of point of contact with respect to the surface remains zero all the times although the centre of the wheel moves forward.
## FLUID FRICTION (DRAG)
Fluids i.e., liquids and gases also a friction on the bodies moving through them.
For a plane to fly, level and at a steady rate, the forces acting on it must be balanced. Lift must equal to weight and thrust must equal to drag. Drag is air resistance to the forward motion of the plane.

## SUMMARY
- Friction : It is the opposing force that produced when two surfaces in contact move relative to each other.
- Static friction : The friction that exists between the surfaces in contact when there is no relative motion. The maximum value of static friction is called limiting friction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∝</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> or, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> coefficient of static friction.
- Kinetic friction : It is the friction exprerienced by a body when it is in motion. It is less than static friction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∝</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> coefficient of kinetic friction.
- Sliding friction : The friction that exists between two surfaces in contact when the body slides on the surface.
- Rolling friction : The friction that exists between two surfaces in contact when the body rolls on the surface. Its magnitude is much less than sliding friction.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∝</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow></math> coefficient of rolling friction.
- Factors that affect friction :
(i) The nature of the surfaces in contact and their state of roughness.
(ii) The force of limiting friction between two surfaces in contact is directly proportional to the normal reaction between the two surface in contact.
(iii) Friction force does not depend on the area of surfaces in contact.
- Angle of friction : The angle which the resultant of the limiting friction and the normal reaction makes with the normal reaction.
Angle of friction, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
- Angle of repose: It is the minimum angle that an inclined plane makes with the horizontal when a body placed on it just begins to slide down.
Angle of repose, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>
- Methods of increasing friction :
(i) Treading of tyres (ii) On a rainy day, sand is thrown on the slippery ground, etc.
- Methods of reducing friction:
(i) By polishing
(ii) By using wheels and ball-bearings
(iii) By lubrication
(iv) By streamlining, etc.
- Fluid friction (Drag) : It is the liquid or air resistance to forward motion of the body.

## FRICTION : A NECESSARY EVIL
Friction has advantages as well as disadvantages. In other words, friction is not desirable but without friction, we cannot think of survival, so we can say that "friction is a necessary evil". In some cases friction acts as a supporting force i.e., as a friend and in some cases it acts as opposing force i.e., as a foe.
## Friction as a Friend / Advantages of Friction :
(i) The force of friction helps us to move on the surface of earth. In the absence of friction, we cannot think of walking on the surface.
(ii) The force of friction between the tip of a pen and the surface of paper helps us to write on the paper. It is not possible to write on the glazed paper as there is no force of friction.
(iii) The force of friction between the tyres of a vehicle and the road helps the vehicle to stop when brake is applied. In the absence of friction, the vehicle skid off the road when brake is applied.
(iv) Moving belts remain on the rim of a wheel because of friction.
(v) The force of friction between a chalk and the blackboard helps us to write on the board.
Fig. 2.8
## Friction as a Foe / Disadvantages of Friction :
(i) A significant amount of energy of a moving object is wasted in the form of heat energy to overcome the force of friction.
(ii) The force of friction restricts the speed of moving vehicles like buses, trains, aeroplanes, rockets etc.
(iii) The efficiency of machines decreases due to the presence of force of friction.
(iv) The force of friction causes lot of wear and tear in the moving parts of a machine.
(v) Sometimes, a machine gets burnt due to the force of friction between different moving parts.

## INCREASING AND REDUCING FRICTION
## Methods of Increasing Friction
- Treading of tyres is done to increase friction between the road and the tyres. Moreover, synthetic rubber is preferred over the natural rubber in the manufacture of tyres because of its larger coefficient of friction with the road.
- Sand is thrown on tracks covered with snow. This increases the force of friction between the wheels and the track and the driving becomes safer.
- On a rainy day, we throw some sand on the slippery ground. This increases the friction between our feet and the ground. This reduces the chances of slipping.
## Methods of Reducing Friction
Friction can be reduced by
- polishing the surface. (but extra polishing increase friction)
- lubrication
- proper selection of material
- avoiding moisture
- streamlining the shape
- using ball bearings or roller bearings
Friction can be considerably reduced by maintaining a thin cushion of compressed air between solid surfaces in relative motion
## Wheel Reduce Friction
When objects such as a wheel (disc or ring), sphere or a cylinder rolls over a surface, the force of friction that comes into play is called rolling friction.
- Rolling friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction ( R ) and inversely proportional to the radius ( r ) of the rolling cylinder or wheel.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mtext>rolling </mtext></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mfrac><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></math> is called coefficient of rolling friction, it would be measured in metre.
- Rolling friction is often quite small as compared to the sliding friction. That is why heavy loads are transported by placing them on carts with wheels.
The velocity of point of contact with respect to the surface remains zero all the times although the centre of the wheel moves forward.
## FLUID FRICTION (DRAG)
Fluids i.e., liquids and gases also a friction on the bodies moving through them.
For a plane to fly, level and at a steady rate, the forces acting on it must be balanced. Lift must equal to weight and thrust must equal to drag. Drag is air resistance to the forward motion of the plane.
